title: De quibusdam eximiis proprietatibus circa divisores potestatum occurrentibus

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes Euler's worked example for a = 30 and begins the summary table (Scholion, §35).

Notation. For a prime p = 2m+1 not dividing a, Euler's criterion gives a^m ≡ ±1 (mod p). The sign is the Legendre symbol (a/p). Euler records the answer through two sets of residues mod 4a, both taken of the form 4k+1:
- T: p ≡ ±T (mod 4a) exactly when p divides a^m − 1.
- Θ: p ≡ ±Θ (mod 4a) exactly when p divides a^m + 1.

In modern terms, (a/p) depends only on p mod 4a and is even under p ↦ −p. That is the content of quadratic reciprocity, which Euler states observationally on the following pages.

Completion of §34 (a = 30 = 2·15).
- The classes for 15, lifted mod 120, are T15 = {1,17,49,53,61,77,109,113} and Θ15 = {13,29,37,41,73,89,97,101}.
- The classes for 2 are: T2 is the numbers ≡ 1 (mod 8), Θ2 is the numbers ≡ 5 (mod 8).
- Since (30/p) = (2/p)(15/p), T30 = (T15∩T2) ∪ (Θ15∩Θ2) = {1,17,49,113} ∪ {13,29,37,101}.
- Θ30 is the complement among residues 4k+1 coprime to 30: {41,53,61,73,77,89,97,109}.
- Spot checks agree: (30/13) = (4/13) = 1, (30/41) = (2/41)(3/41)(5/41) = −1.
- The rule used is multiplicativity of the symbol in its upper argument.

Scholion §35. A table for all non-square a ≤ 30: a = 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 appear on this page; the rest on the next. It gives the classes mod 4a of primes dividing a^m − 1 versus a^m + 1.
- Square factors are absorbed: 8 behaves like 2, 12 like 3, 18 like 2, 20 like 5. The listed residues are just those for the squarefree part, restricted to numbers coprime to a.
- I checked every row on this page against modern Legendre-symbol computation. All are correct except the omission noted below.
- In each row the two lists have φ(4a)/4 entries each, i.e. half the classes of 4k+1 type. Together with ± they exhaust (Z/4a)*.

The purpose of the table is to support the two 'conclusiones ex observationibus' that Euler wants proved. On the next pages these become theorems on prime divisors of xx ∓ ayy, i.e. Euler's form of quadratic reciprocity.
errors: Row a = 14, second line: printed '56.s ∓ 17, 29, 33, 37, 41,' omits 53. The Θ-set for a = 14 must have 6 elements, matching the 6 T-elements, to fill φ(56)/2 = 12 classes with ±. Directly, (14/53) = (2/53)(7/53) = (−1)(53/7) = (−1)(4/7) = −1. The previous page (§32, 3°) correctly gives Θ = 17, 29, 33, 37, 41, 53, so this is a copying or typesetting slip in the summary table.
No other errors found. Rows for a = 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 and the a = 30 computation all check correctly.

ideas.what: Classification of primes p by whether p | a^m − 1 or p | a^m + 1 (p = 2m+1) via residue classes ±T, ±Θ mod 4a
ideas.modern_name: Euler's criterion plus quadratic reciprocity: (a/p) depends only on p mod 4a and is even under p → −p
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (observational formulation, E164 / E552 / E557); first proof by Gauss 1796/1801
ideas.where_published: E164 (Theoremata circa divisores numerorum in hac forma paa±qbb contentorum); Opuscula analytica 1783 papers including E557; discussed in Weil, Number Theory, and Lemmermeyer, Reciprocity Laws

ideas.what: Computing T, Θ for composite a by intersecting classes of its factors (T∩T ∪ Θ∩Θ)
ideas.modern_name: Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol in the numerator, (ab/p) = (a/p)(b/p); character product on (Z/4a)*
ideas.where_published: E557 §§32–34; implicit in earlier Euler number-theory papers

ideas.what: Square factors of a can be dropped (a = ffg behaves like g, with p coprime to f)

deep.surprise_reason: These are Euler's well-known tables underlying his empirical statement of quadratic reciprocity, which is standard in the historical literature. The only notable item is a minor misprint: 53 is omitted from the a = 14 Θ-row.
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reflects the printed omission in row 14 (Θ: 17, 29, 33, 37, 41,); the mathematically correct row adds 53, as on page 290.
